header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
Tajamul Mukhtar etc. Vs. The State, etc.
Order with signature of judge, and that of parties or counsel,
18.11.2026. Mr. Rizwan Khalid, Advocate with petitioners.
Mr. Hamaad Iftikhar Syed, DDPP with Usman ASI.
Mehar Ali Raza Sadiq, Advocate for complainant.
body: Tajamal Mukhtar, Tahamal Mukhtar and Shafqat Mukhtar (petitioners), through this criminal revision under Sections 435 and 439, Cr.P.C., have called in question the legality of the order dated 17.06.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Sahiwal, whereby an application moved by respondent No.2/complainant (Mst. Asiya Arshad) for cancellation of pre-arrest bail, earlier confirmed in favour of the petitioners vide order dated 22.12.2025, was accepted and the concession of pre-arrest bail extended to the petitioners was recalled 2. The brief facts necessary for adjudication of the instant revision are that a criminal case [ ] was registered against the present petitioners at the instance of respondent No.2. During the course of investigation, the investigating officer initially found Sections 452 and 342, PPC not attracted to the facts of the case and deleted the same [ ]. The petitioners approached the competent Court for the grant of pre-arrest bail and, after hearing the parties, their bail was confirmed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge on 22.12.2025.

3. Subsequently, respondent No.2 questioned the investigation and the matter was entrusted to a superior police officer for further inquiry. After conducting further investigation and inspecting the place of occurrence, the DSP [ ] FIR No.1102/25 dated 01.11.2025, Police Station Dera Rahim, District Sahiwal, under Sections 337-A(i), 337-F(i), 452, 342, 354 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, [ ] This fact was recorded in Zimni No.6 (case diary) dated 29.11.2025. reached a different conclusion regarding the residential arrangement of the parties and restored the allegation under Section 452, PPC [ ]. The complainant thereafter moved an application for cancellation of the petitioners' pre-arrest bail, which was dismissed for non-prosecution on 26.02.2026. A subsequent application for the same relief was filed on 07.03.2026 and, vide the impugned order dated 17.06.2026, the learned Additional Sessions Judge accepted the same, principally on the ground that the factual premise underlying the earlier confirmation of bail had subsequently been found incorrect during further investigation. Hence, the instant revision.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that the impugned order is the result of misreading and non-reading of the material available on record and has been passed without appreciating the distinction between the grant of bail and its subsequent cancellation. It is argued that the earlier concession of pre-arrest bail was extended after consideration of the available material, whereas no subsequent conduct attributable to the petitioners has been brought on record to demonstrate misuse of the concession. Learned counsel further submits that the subsequent alteration of the investigation by the DSP, particularly the restoration of Section 452, PPC, cannot automatically furnish a lawful ground for cancellation of bail, especially when the allegations and circumstances forming the basis of the FIR were already available at the time of confirmation of bail. It is also pointed out that the complainant had earlier moved an application for cancellation of bail, which was dismissed for non-prosecution, but this material circumstance was not properly appreciated by the learned Court below. [ ] This fact finds its existence in Zimni No.11 (case diary) dated 20.01.2026.
5. Conversely, learned counsel for respondent No.2 and the learned Law Officer oppose the revision and support the impugned order.

7. Before examining the controversy on merits, it would be appropriate to reiterate that the considerations governing the grant of bail are materially different from those governing its cancellation. Once an accused has been admitted to bail by a competent Court, the concession so extended cannot be withdrawn in a routine manner or merely because another view of the available material is possible [ ]. The jurisdiction relating to cancellation of bail is to be exercised with circumspection and only where the case falls within the recognized parameters laid down by the superior Courts. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has, on numerous occasions, enumerated the circumstances in which an order granting bail may be recalled, including where the order is patently illegal, erroneous or factually incorrect and has resulted in a miscarriage of justice, or where the accused has misused the concession of bail, attempted to influence or pressurize the prosecution witnesses, is likely to abscond, has interfered with the investigation, has indulged in a similar offence while on bail, or where fresh facts and material collected during the investigation tend to establish his guilt [ ].

8. Adverting to the facts of the instant case, it is evident that the petitioners were initially admitted to pre-arrest bail after the investigating officer had deleted Sections 452 and 342, PPC from the case. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, while confirming the concession on 22.12.2025, took into consideration the investigation conducted at that stage and the circumstances emerging therefrom. Subsequently, the [ ] Tariq Bashir and 5 others v. The State (PLD 1995 SC 34); Sami Ullah and another v. Laiq Zada and another (2020 SCMR 1115); Suba Khan v. Muhammad Ajmal and 2 others (2006 SCMR 66); Munir Ahmad v. The State and another (2014 SCMR 1669). [ ] Sami Ullah and another v. Laiq Zada and another (supra); Ali Asghar Khokhar v. Anwar Ali Kori and another (2026 S C M R 1963).

complainant challenged the investigation, whereupon the DSP conducted a further inquiry and restored the allegation under Section 452, PPC. The learned Court below treated this subsequent development as sufficient, in itself, to recall the concession of bail. The mere fact that a superior police officer has reached a conclusion different from that of the earlier investigating officer does not dispense with the requirement of examining whether the subsequent material actually satisfies the recognised legal grounds for cancellation of bail, particularly as the opinion of the police is not binding on the Court [ ]. In the present case, the principal development relied upon by the complainant is the restoration of Section 452, PPC. The inquiry conducted by the DSP appears to have proceeded on the premise that the complainant was residing in a separate house and was not sharing a common residence with the petitioners. This circumstance may have relevance while examining the applicability of Section 452, PPC; however, it cannot, without further assessment of the underlying material, be treated as conclusive proof of the commission of the alleged offence or of the involvement of the petitioners therein. At the stage of cancellation of bail, the Court is not expected to embark upon a detailed appraisal of such disputed factual questions or to record findings which may prejudice either side at trial [ ]. The learned Court below ought to have confined itself to determining whether the subsequent material was sufficient, in law, to justify cancellation of bail, rather than treating the altered conclusion of the investigating officer as determinative of the matter. There is nothing in the material presently brought to the notice of this Court to indicate that, after confirmation of their pre-arrest bail, the petitioners attempted to influence or intimidate the complainant or any other prosecution witness, tampered with the evidence, interfered with the investigation, absconded from the process of law or indulged in any similar criminal activity. No specific [ ] Allah Dewayo Shahani v. The State through Prosecutor General, Sindh (2023 SCMR 1724), para 5. [ ] Muhammad Sarfraz Ansari v. The State and others (PLD 2021 SC 738). instance of misuse of the concession of bail has been identified in the impugned order. Although proof of misuse is not the only recognized ground for cancellation, in its absence the Court was required to examine with greater care whether the subsequent investigation had rendered the original bail order patently erroneous or factually unsustainable.

9. For the foregoing reasons, this Court is of the considered view that the impugned order dated 17.06.2026 cannot be sustained in the eyes of law. The subsequent restoration of Section 452, PPC, without an adequate examination of the underlying material and its legal significance, was not, in the circumstances of the present case, sufficient to justify cancellation of the concession of pre-arrest bail earlier confirmed in favour of the petitioners. The impugned order, therefore, suffers from material mis-appreciation of the record and warrants interference by this Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. Consequently, the instant criminal revision is allowed. The impugned order dated 17.06.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Sahiwal, is hereby set aside and the application for cancellation of prearrest bail filed by respondent No.2 stands dismissed. Resultantly, the order dated 22.12.2025, whereby pre-arrest bail was confirmed in favour of the petitioners, is restored and shall remain operative, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Needless to observe, the observations made hereinabove are tentative in nature and shall not influence the learned trial Court while conducting the trial or deciding any matter arising therefrom.
JUDGE Umar Hayat* APPROVED FOR REPORTING (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz)
